name: Phrygian
confidence_why: Obrador-Cursach 2020, Šorgo 2026 and Diakonoff and Neroznak 1985 all state that the Phrygian scripts mark no accent and that the position of the stress is unknown; Šorgo 2026 adds only that two vowel reductions point to a stress-based rather than pitch accent, without fixing where it fell.

catalog_quote: There are two hypothetical explanations for this unexpected result: in an early prehistoric stage of the language the laryngeal dropped in final position ... or the shift *e > a only worked on stressed position. However, neither is conclusive: more examples of such dropping are lacking and our knowledge of the nature and position of the Phrygian stress is insufficient.

audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation is verbatim in the Obrador-Cursach 2020 text we hold at p. 75, and both supporting remarks (p. 51 clitics; lexicon pp. 327-328 πατερης/πατρες) are where the record says. (2) The source is the 2020 Brill handbook, the standard and most comprehensive description of Phrygian; the held Ligorio & Lubotsky 2018 HSK sketch adds only 'presumably in pretonic position' for e/i vacillation and Wackernagel placement after 'the first accented word', neither giving a position rule. sources.citation: Diakonoff, I. M. and V. P. Neroznak. 1985. Phrygian. Delmar, NY: Caravan Books. xx+149 pp.
sources.quote: Passing assumption only, in a comparison with Armenian: 'a changeover from the I.-E. system of tones and mobile stress which apparently continued to obtain in Phrygian, to strong expiratory stress fixed on the penultimate syllable' [in Armenian]. Elsewhere stress is invoked ad hoc for vowel reflexes ('after stress *a, *e > [a?]'). No rule for Phrygian stress position is stated or argued.
sources.note: Glottolog-listed sketch (xx+149 pp.); only a passing assumption that IE mobile accent 'apparently continued' in Phrygian (p. 42); useful as the one older source that ventures a view.

sources.citation: Obrador Cursach, Bartomeu. 2018. Lexicon of the Phrygian Inscriptions. PhD thesis, Universitat de Barcelona (Facultat de Filologia), 575 pp.http://hdl.handle.net/2445/124508(= TDXhttp://hdl.handle.net/10803/650834).
sources.note: No statement on tone or pitch anywhere in the thesis (no hits for tone/tonal/pitch). Prosody content is limited to stress: p.50 clitics are written together with 'the stressed words'; p.59 the e~i spelling hesitation is best explained as 'pretonic neutralisation' (following Ligorio & Lubotsky 2013: 187) rather than Brixhe's hiatus neutralisation; p.67 'our knowledge of the nature and position of the Phrygian stress is insufficient'; p.267 πατρες vs πατερης shows syncope 'in the syllable where the stress would be expected', so the stress 'must have changed its position'.

tone.quote: There are many hesitations between ‹e› and ‹i› in Phrygian ... Although it has been unanimously considered a phonetic hesitation between /e/ and /i/, the two given analyses are very different: Brixhe (2008, 75) identifies neutralisation of the contrast of /e/ and /i/ in hiatus (as in δεως passim ~ διως 12.1 = 121, etc.), while Ligorio and Lubotsky (2013, 187) prefer to speak about a pretonic neutralisation. The second explanation is better because it accounts for all occurrences of such a hesitation. ... [p. 67:] However, neither is conclusive: more examples of such dropping are lacking and our knowledge of the nature and position of the Phrygian stress is insufficient.
tone.summary: Accent of unknown nature and position; pretonic e~i neutralisation assumed; nothing on tone.

tone.quote: In general, hesitations between /e/ and /i/ are attested in Phrygian under different conditions: some instances may be due to pre-nasal raising (akenanogavos [M-01a and W-01a] ~ akinanogavan [M-04]), while others may involve pretonic or post-tonic weakening (kubeleya [B-01] ~ kubileya [W-04], αββερετορ [Haas 1966, nos. 73, 75] ~ αββιρετο [Haas 1966, no. 25]), and still others show this variation in the root vowel (δεως ~ διως [Haas 1966, nos. 4, 5, 39]; cf. also -βερ- ~ -βιρ- above). Thus βρικίσματα (Hsch.) might display the raising of /e/ to /i/ in pretonic position.
tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.summary: Accent-conditioned (pre-/post-tonic) weakening of /e/ assumed; nothing on tone.

sources.citation: Brixhe, Claude. 1993. Du paléo- au néo-phrygien. Comptes rendus des séances de l'Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres 137(2): 323-344.

tone.quote: Le conservatisme inhérent au caractère souvent formulaire des textes favorise une remarquable stabilité des formes écrites et permet de vérifier aisément, à travers une série de correspondances, que ces deux ensembles documentaires correspondent à deux états d'une même langue ; ainsi : — passage de o final à u devant nasale, p.p. bagun (G- 136) ... — *e: hérité >a:, p.p. matar (e.g. W-04) ... [p. 343:] on maîtrise, en effet, de larges pans de la phonétique, de la morphologie et de la syntaxe.
tone.locator: p. 330 (§5 'Du paléo- au néo-phrygien', opening list of sound correspondences) and p. 343 (§10 Conclusion)
tone.translation: The conservatism inherent in the often formulaic character of the texts favours a remarkable stability of the written forms and makes it easy to verify, through a series of correspondences, that these two documentary sets correspond to two states of one and the same language; thus: — passage of final o to u before a nasal, Old Phr. bagun (G-136) ... — inherited *ē > ā, Old Phr. matar (e.g. W-04) ... [p. 343:] indeed, large parts of the phonetics, morphology and syntax are under control.
tone.summary: No prosodic content: OPhr.>NPhr. segmental correspondences and morphology only; accent never mentioned.
